title: Judge blocks Trump’s FCC from targeting ABC stations: ‘This is not a close case’ | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

Siding with Disney in a dramatic First Amendment case, a federal judge has barred the Trump administration from taking further action against ABC’s local TV stations.

On Wednesday, US District Judge Loren AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction that Disney has been seeking against the Federal Communications Commission, chaired by Brendan Carr, a close ally of President Donald Trump.

“This is not a close case,” AliKhan wrote in her decision, which also denied the FCC’s motion to dismiss Disney’s lawsuit.

The injunction means that the FCC can’t continue its early review of ABC’s station licenses while the legal process plays out.

After weighing the evidence, the judge concluded that Disney’s lawyers “sufficiently cast the early license renewal proceedings as a retaliatory act.”

The ruling is a clear victory for Disney, whichwent to courtin August to defend its ABC stations from the FCC’s pressure campaign.

The stations fall under the FCC’s purview because they broadcast over the public airwaves.

Disney’s lawsuit documented the FCC’s unusual steps to investigate and challenge ABC’s stations. “The administration has steadily increased the pressure” on ABC, the suit stated, “culminating in the present threat to the broadcasting licenses of the eight ABC owned stations.”

ABC’s licenses weren’t due for renewal for several years, but in April, Carr ordered the company to file early-renewal paperwork, something that the FCC virtually never does.

At the same time, Trump publicly pressured ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, and the network ignored his demands.

Carr claimed that the license review was related to an ongoing FCC probe of Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts.

But former FCC officials said that explanation didn’t make sense, and Disney argued that it was just a pretext. Disney said the court’s intervention was necessary to stop an “extraordinary assault on free speech.”

AliKhan heard arguments from both sides in October. FCC lawyers argued that the District Court lacked jurisdiction, but on Wednesday she wrote that Disney had established jurisdiction.

“No one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”

AliKhan wrote that Carr “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders,” and “it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”

An ABC spokesperson said: “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration.”

In a statement, an FCC spokesperson said the “decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law,” and said the commission “looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”

But the FCC’s lone Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, cheered the judge’s decision, saying it showed that “this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights.”

Gomez, who publicly supported Disney’s lawsuit, said, “For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct.”

Gomez urged other broadcasters to “take note” and follow Disney’s lead.
